subject: Everyday Science
q: Quicklime is:
explanation: Quicklime (CaO) is made by heating limestone; adding water to it produces slaked lime, calcium hydroxide.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The gas commonly called “laughing gas” is:
explanation: Nitrous oxide (N2O) produces euphoria when inhaled and is used as a mild anaesthetic, especially in dentistry.

subject: Everyday Science
q: “Dry ice” is the solid form of:
explanation: Solid carbon dioxide is called dry ice because it turns directly into gas at −78.5 °C without melting into a liquid.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The direct change of a solid into a gas without becoming a liquid, as with naphthalene balls, is called:
explanation: In sublimation, particles escape straight from the solid into the vapour; naphthalene, camphor and dry ice all behave this way.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which strong-smelling substance is added to LPG so that leaks can be detected?
explanation: LPG itself is odourless, so a small amount of a sulphur compound, ethyl mercaptan, is added to give it a distinct smell.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Nail polish remover commonly contains:
explanation: Acetone is a good solvent that dissolves the film-forming resins of nail polish and evaporates quickly.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Non-stick cooking utensils are coated with:
explanation: Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene) is heat-resistant and has very low friction, so food does not stick to it.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Gunpowder is a mixture of potassium nitrate, charcoal and:
explanation: Black powder combines potassium nitrate (oxidiser) with charcoal and sulphur (fuels), which burn rapidly together.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Brass is an alloy of:
explanation: Brass is made by combining copper with zinc; it is harder than copper and resists corrosion.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bronze is an alloy of:
explanation: Bronze, one of the earliest alloys used by humans, is mainly copper with tin, which makes it harder than pure copper.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Stainless steel resists rusting mainly because it contains:
explanation: Chromium forms a thin, tough oxide layer on the surface that prevents oxygen and moisture from reaching the iron.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Steel is an alloy of iron and:
explanation: Adding a small amount of carbon to iron makes steel, which is much stronger and harder than pure iron.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Galvanisation of iron means coating it with a layer of:
explanation: Zinc protects iron both as a barrier and because it corrodes in preference to iron, so galvanised sheets and pipes resist rusting.

subject: Everyday Science
q: For iron to rust, it must be exposed to:
explanation: Rusting is the reaction of iron with oxygen in the presence of moisture; iron kept in dry air or in air-free water does not rust.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bauxite is the chief ore of:
explanation: Bauxite is rich in aluminium oxide; the oxide is purified and then electrolysed to obtain aluminium.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Haematite is an ore of:
explanation: Haematite is iron(III) oxide, one of the most important ores smelted in blast furnaces to produce iron.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which metal is a liquid at ordinary room temperature?
explanation: Mercury melts at about −39 °C, so it is liquid at room temperature, unlike other common metals.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The most abundant metal in the Earth’s crust is:
explanation: Aluminium makes up about 8% of the crust by mass, more than any other metal; oxygen and silicon, the most abundant elements, are non-metals.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
explanation: Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of all metals, but copper is used for wiring because it is much cheaper.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Copper is widely used for electric wires mainly because it:
o: Is the best conductor of all metals
Conducts electricity well and can be drawn into thin wires
explanation: Copper combines high conductivity with ductility and reasonable cost, making it ideal for household and industrial wiring.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Solder, traditionally used to join electrical wires, is an alloy of:
explanation: Tin–lead solder melts at a low temperature, so it can join metal parts without melting them; lead-free tin alloys are now common.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sodium metal is stored under kerosene because it:
o: Reacts vigorously with air and water
explanation: Sodium reacts rapidly with oxygen and violently with moisture, so it is kept under kerosene, with which it does not react.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Noble gases such as neon and argon are very unreactive because:
o: Their outermost electron shells are full
explanation: A complete outer shell is a stable arrangement, so these atoms have little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Filament bulbs are filled with an inert gas such as argon mainly to:
o: Prevent the hot filament from burning away
Increase the brightness of the colour
explanation: In air the white-hot tungsten filament would oxidise quickly; an unreactive gas such as argon slows its evaporation and burning.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Airships and weather balloons are filled with helium rather than hydrogen because helium is:
explanation: Hydrogen is lighter but burns explosively; helium is also much lighter than air and, being a noble gas, does not burn.

subject: Everyday Science
q: PVC, a plastic used for pipes, stands for:
explanation: PVC is polyvinyl chloride, a polymer of vinyl chloride used for pipes, cable insulation and flooring.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following is a natural polymer?
explanation: Cellulose, found in plant cell walls, cotton and wood, is a natural polymer of glucose; the others are synthetic.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which fibre is known as “artificial silk”?
explanation: Rayon is made from regenerated wood cellulose and has a silk-like shine and feel, hence its name.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Plastics that soften on heating and can be remoulded again and again are called:
explanation: Thermoplastics such as polythene and PVC have chains that are not cross-linked, so heat softens them repeatedly.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bakelite, used for electrical switches and handles, is a:
explanation: Once set, Bakelite’s cross-linked structure does not soften on reheating, and it insulates against heat and electricity.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Polythene is made by the polymerisation of:
explanation: Many ethene (ethylene) molecules join end to end to form the long chains of polyethylene.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Vulcanisation of rubber involves heating it with:
explanation: Sulphur forms cross-links between rubber chains, making the rubber harder, more elastic and more durable, as in tyres.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ordinary cement is manufactured mainly from:
explanation: Limestone and clay are heated together in a kiln to form clinker, which is ground with a little gypsum to make cement.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of:
explanation: Soap is made by boiling fats or oils with an alkali (saponification), producing salts of long-chain fatty acids.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Detergents help clean clothes mainly by:
o: Reducing the surface tension of water
explanation: Lowering surface tension lets water wet fabric more thoroughly, while detergent molecules surround grease so it can be rinsed away.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which gas is commonly used in fire extinguishers?
explanation: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and does not burn or support burning, so it blankets the fire and cuts off oxygen.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The chemical symbol of potassium is:
explanation: The symbol K comes from kalium, the Latin name for potassium; P is phosphorus, Po polonium and Pt platinum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Silicon, used in computer chips, is classified by its electrical behaviour as a:
explanation: Silicon conducts electricity better than an insulator but far less than a metal, and its conductivity can be controlled by adding impurities.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Coating a metal object with a thin layer of another metal using electricity is called:
explanation: In electroplating, the object is made the cathode in a solution of the coating metal’s salt, so metal is deposited on it when current flows.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In the Haber process, ammonia is manufactured from:
explanation: Nitrogen from air and hydrogen react over an iron catalyst at high pressure to form ammonia, the basis of most nitrogen fertilisers.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without itself being used up is called a:
explanation: A catalyst provides an easier reaction pathway and is recovered unchanged at the end, so small amounts can be used again and again.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The property of some substances to absorb moisture from the air and dissolve in it is called:
explanation: Deliquescent substances such as calcium chloride or sodium hydroxide absorb so much water vapour that they form a solution; efflorescence is the opposite, the loss of water.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In chemistry, oxidation is defined as:
o: Loss of oxygen or gain of electrons
Gain of oxygen or loss of electrons
explanation: Oxidation means adding oxygen, removing hydrogen or, most generally, losing electrons; reduction is the reverse.

subject: Everyday Science
q: According to Ohm’s law, if the resistance of a conductor stays the same and the voltage across it is doubled, the current will:
explanation: Ohm’s law says current is directly proportional to voltage when resistance (and temperature) remain constant.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Household appliances are connected in parallel mainly because:
o: Each receives the full mains voltage and can be switched on or off independently
It reduces the voltage to each appliance
Current then flows through every appliance in turn
explanation: In a parallel circuit each branch is connected directly across the supply, so appliances work at full voltage and one failing does not switch off the others.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A device that automatically cuts off a circuit when too much current flows, and can simply be reset afterwards, is a:
explanation: A circuit breaker trips a switch during an overload or short circuit and can be switched back on; a fuse melts and must be replaced.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The wire used in an electric fuse should have:
explanation: When excess current flows, the fuse wire heats up and melts quickly, breaking the circuit before the wiring or appliance is damaged.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The earth wire in household wiring is provided to:
o: Supply extra power to heavy appliances
Carry leakage current safely to the ground
explanation: If a live wire touches a metal casing, the earth wire gives the current an easy path to the ground, blowing the fuse and preventing electric shock.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The electricity supplied to homes through the mains is:
explanation: Mains electricity is alternating current, which can be stepped up or down easily with transformers for efficient transmission.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The frequency of the mains electricity supply in Pakistan is:
explanation: Pakistan, like most of Asia and Europe, uses alternating current at 50 hertz (with a nominal voltage of about 220–230 V); North America uses 60 Hz.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A device that converts alternating current into direct current is called a:
explanation: A rectifier, usually built from diodes, lets current pass in only one direction, turning AC into DC for chargers and electronic devices.

subject: Everyday Science
q: If output voltage is greater than input voltage, then transformer is:
explanation: A step-up transformer has more turns on its secondary coil than on its primary, so it raises the voltage.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A transformer works only with alternating current because:
o: Direct current would melt its core
Its coils are made of copper
It needs a changing magnetic field to induce voltage in the secondary coil
explanation: Only a current that keeps changing produces a changing magnetic field; a steady direct current would induce no voltage in the second coil.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Electricity is transmitted over long distances at very high voltage in order to:
o: Increase the current in the wires
Make the lines safer to touch
Reduce energy lost as heat in the wires
Raise the frequency of the supply
explanation: For the same power, a higher voltage means a smaller current, and a smaller current wastes far less energy as heat in the cables.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An electric motor converts:
explanation: In a motor, current in a coil placed in a magnetic field experiences a force that makes the coil turn.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An electric generator works on the principle of:
explanation: Rotating a coil in a magnetic field changes the magnetic field through it, which induces a voltage and drives a current.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Electromagnetic induction was discovered by:
explanation: In 1831 Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field produces an electric current in a nearby circuit, the basis of generators and transformers.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Lightning conductors are fixed on tall buildings to:
o: Conduct the lightning discharge safely into the ground
explanation: A pointed metal rod connected to the earth gives lightning an easy path to the ground, so the current does not pass through the building.

subject: Everyday Science
q: When a plastic comb is rubbed on dry hair it becomes charged because:
o: Protons move from the hair to the comb
Electrons are transferred between the comb and the hair
explanation: Friction moves electrons from one material to the other, leaving one negatively and the other positively charged; protons do not move.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A diode is an electronic component that allows current to flow:
explanation: A diode conducts easily in its forward direction and blocks current in the reverse direction, which is why it is used in rectifiers.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Superconductors are materials that:
o: Have zero electrical resistance below a certain very low temperature
Store electric charge like a battery
Allow current in one direction only
explanation: Cooled below their critical temperature, superconductors carry current with no resistance, which is used in powerful MRI magnets.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The resistance of a metal wire generally ______ when its temperature rises.
explanation: Heating makes the metal ions vibrate more strongly, so the moving electrons collide with them more often and resistance rises.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The heating elements of electric irons and heaters are commonly made of:
explanation: Nichrome, an alloy of nickel and chromium, has high resistance and does not oxidise easily when red-hot.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The filament of an incandescent electric bulb is made of:
explanation: Tungsten has the highest melting point of all metals (about 3,400 °C), so it can glow white-hot without melting.

subject: Everyday Science
q: When the north poles of two magnets are brought close together, they:
o: Have no effect on each other
explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract; this is the basic law of magnetic poles.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A freely suspended bar magnet always comes to rest pointing:
explanation: The Earth behaves like a huge magnet, so a free magnet aligns itself with the Earth’s magnetic field, roughly north–south; this is how a compass works.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An electromagnet loses most of its magnetism when:
o: The coil is given more turns
explanation: An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows in its coil, which is why it is used in cranes, bells and relays that must switch on and off.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Soft iron is used for the core of an electromagnet because it:
explanation: Soft iron becomes strongly magnetic when current flows and loses its magnetism quickly when switched off, unlike steel, which stays magnetised.

subject: Everyday Science
q: MRI scanners form images of the body using:
o: A strong magnetic field and radio waves
explanation: Magnetic resonance imaging aligns hydrogen nuclei in a strong magnetic field and detects the radio signals they give off, so no ionising radiation is used.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Maglev trains are able to float just above their track because of:
explanation: Powerful magnets lift and propel the train, so there is no wheel-on-rail friction, allowing very high speeds.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sound cannot travel through:
explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles of a medium to vibrate, so it cannot pass through empty space.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sound waves in air are:
explanation: In a sound wave the air particles vibrate back and forth along the direction in which the wave travels, forming compressions and rarefactions.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The pitch of a sound depends on its:
explanation: A higher frequency of vibration is heard as a higher pitch; amplitude decides loudness instead.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The loudness of a sound depends mainly on its:
explanation: Larger vibrations carry more energy and are heard as louder sounds.

subject: Everyday Science
q: We can recognise a familiar person by voice alone, even in the dark, because of the sound’s:
explanation: The mixture of overtones in a voice gives it a characteristic quality or timbre, which lets us distinguish voices even at the same pitch and loudness.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The normal range of frequencies audible to the human ear is about:
explanation: Most people hear from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz; lower frequencies are infrasound and higher ones ultrasound.
